Paper: Ge et al., Doc2Harness, arXiv 2610.20344 (listed 14 to 15 Oct 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20344
Site: https://geyuyao.com/doc2harness
Facts and connections: fact-ledger.md
Rule: one claim plus one image per beat, image right under the tweet that uses it, one-line caption, text explains and the image carries the numbers.

Tweet 1

Doc2Harness is a new test that asks an AI to build a coding harness from a written spec, then grades the harness it built. Most coding tests keep the harness fixed and only score the task. This one flips it.

Even the best model fails almost half the checks.

Tweet 2

A harness is the small program around a model: its tools, its permissions, its memory of the session, how it runs commands, and when it stops. Same model, different harness, different results. An earlier test, Claw-SWE-Bench, found switching harness moves scores almost as much as switching model.

Tweet 3

How it works, in two stages.

Stage 1: the model gets a design document and a short empty outline of the code. It writes the whole harness itself, inside a sealed test machine.

Stage 2: freeze that harness. Drive it with a scripted fake model instead of a real AI. Check only what you can see from outside: what it sends, what files it writes, how it exits, what it prints.

Tweet 4

The design document combines behavior from twelve harnesses people already use, like Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex CLI (command line interface), Cursor, and Aider. Conflicting rules were cleaned up first. Every model builds inside the same tool, OpenCode, so no company's own tool favors its own model.

A typical finished harness is about 30 files. Almost all of it is new code from the model.

Tweet 5

They also guard against fake passes. Example: a check that the harness refused to read a file outside its folder. A harness that can't read any file at all would also pass. So a "positive control" first checks that a normal read works.

The chart shows which kinds of checks have that guard most often.

Tweet 6

Ranks jump a lot by category. A model can be near the top on file handling and near the bottom on session memory.

Permissions split strong and weak models the most. The live-terminal category is close to solved, so it barely separates anyone.

Tweet 7

Where it breaks. Bigger harnesses don't score better. With the same amount of code, harnesses split into more modules score lower. Failures cluster where shared behavior is spread across files.

Tweet 8

This changes how I read two papers we covered. STITCH builds a harness for each task from a library of small, tested parts. Growing Harness has a model edit harness code after each failure and keeps only edits that don't hurt held-out tasks.

Both assume the model can write harness code that does what it claims. Doc2Harness tests that directly, and the answer is "only about half the time." It also explains why both papers keep the model's edits small and checked.

Tweet 9

And it fits Fan et al. on harness design: the shape of the code around a model matters about as much as the model. Here, the shape the model chooses for itself is where it fails.

Tweet 10

Limits the paper owns. Each model gets one build with at most three submissions, not a build, test, fix loop. Related checks can fail together from one bug. And it measures whether the harness follows the written rules, not whether a real coding assistant would ship more working code with it.

What I still don't know: would a model that can run the tests and retry close most of this gap?

Tweet 11

If you build coding assistants: don't treat the harness as a fixed wrapper. Check that the one you build, or let a model build, actually obeys permissions, session rules, and folder limits when tested from outside.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20344
